items.prompt: Roads are built one at a time between n towns. After each road, report how many separate regions remain.
items.why: Groups only merge and you must answer after every link → union-find with a component counter. A traversal per road is O(n) each.

items.prompt: Courses have prerequisites (a must come before b). Decide whether all courses can be finished.
items.why: Directed dependencies → topological sort (Kahn's in-degrees or DFS colours). Union-find ignores direction and can't see a directed cycle.

items.prompt: Each account is a name plus emails; two accounts belong to the same person if they share any email. Merge the accounts.
items.why: "Shares something" is a transitive link → union the emails (dict-based parent), then group by root.

items.prompt: Count the islands in a fixed grid of land and water.
items.why: Static grid, one question → a flood fill from each unvisited land cell is the simplest tool. Union-find pays off only when land is added over time.

items.prompt: Given equations like "a==b" and "b!=c" over single-letter variables, decide whether all of them can hold at once.
items.why: Union all '==' pairs first, then any '!=' pair with the same root is a contradiction. No search is needed.

items.prompt: Find the fewest moves for a knight to go from one square to another on an empty board.
items.why: Fewest steps where every move costs 1 → BFS. Union-find only says whether a path exists, not how long it is.

items.prompt: Connect all n offices with cables at minimum total cost, given the cost of every possible cable.
items.why: Minimum spanning tree → Kruskal: sort the cables by cost and keep each one whose union succeeds. Shortest paths minimise a route between two points, not the total cost of connecting everyone.

items.prompt: Flights have prices; find the cheapest route from city A to city B.
items.why: Weighted edges + minimise the path cost → Dijkstra. Plain BFS assumes equal weights.

items.prompt: A tree had one extra undirected edge added. Find an edge you can remove to restore the tree.
items.why: Process edges in order; the first one whose ends already share a root closes the cycle. That's O(α(n)) per edge.
